title: String char-indices vs. byte offsets: fix implementation to match actual API contract
context: tree-sitter returns offsets as UTF-16 code-unit indices (JS string indices), but the fields are named `*Byte`, suggesting UTF-8 byte offsets. The implementation treated them as bytes, corrupting output for any non-ASCII content before a mutation target (UTF-8 byte length ≠ UTF-16 code-unit count). Touches invariant(s): con_039cee7367 (Memory hygiene is the agent's job, done without waiting for the human: accept shipped roadmap proposals, settle provenance-repair escalations (apply the true commit or drop), re-anchor or stale findings, and land the resulting capture commits through a PR. Only decisions that need genuine product judgment are queued for the human.).
decision: Renamed `spliceBytes()` to `spliceChars()` and re-implemented as plain string slicing. The offsets are what they actually are (char indices), so fix the implementation to match the contract, not the misleading field names. Added a doc comment explaining the discrepancy for future maintainers.
consequences: Non-ASCII content in source files is now handled correctly during mutation splicing
Naming debt remains: fields still say `*Byte` but mean char-indices — a follow-up rename would be desirable but is a separate concern
Reduced cognitive load: implementation now obviously matches the actual values flowing through the code
alternatives_rejected: Refactor tree-sitter wrapper to convert offsets to true UTF-8 bytes (more invasive, slower, unnecessary since JS works in char-indices)
Rename all `*Byte` fields to `*Char` across the codebase (widespread refactoring, high friction, not the blocking bug)
Keep Buffer-based approach and try to compensate for encoding differences (fragile, error-prone, ongoing maintenance hazard)
